a: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite
p: A new speaker, never mentioned before or after, with the fullest family line of anyone in the debate.
b: Elihu means "He is my God," a form of the name Elijah. Barachel means "God blesses." Buz was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and a brother of Uz, Job's homeland (Genesis 22:21); Jeremiah lists Buz with Dedan and Tema, desert peoples of Arabia (Jeremiah 25:23). Ram is a name in Judah's line (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chronicles 2:9), which is why the Talmud asks whether Elihu was an Israelite (Bava Batra 15b). The Old Greek adds that he was "of the country of Ausitis," that is, of Uz, Job's own land, a plus that Origen marked with an obelus as not in the Hebrew. The prologue does not name him, the LORD does not mention him in 42:7–9, and the epilogue leaves him out. Every reading of the book has to explain that.
r: Genesis 22:20–21; Jeremiah 25:23; Ruth 4:19; 1 Chronicles 2:9; 1 Samuel 1:1; 1 Chronicles 27:18

a: blazed up
p: The narrator says Elihu's anger "blazed" four times in four verses.
b: Wayyichar appo, "his nose burned," is the usual Hebrew idiom for anger. The narrator uses it four times in 32:2–5, more than for any other character in the book. Some readers take it as a portrait of zeal for God's honor; others hear a hint that this young man is speaking out of temper. The same idiom returns when the LORD's anger "burns" against Eliphaz and his friends (42:7), and Elihu is not named there.

a: because he held himself in the right rather than God
t: Right instead of God, or right before God?
p: The Hebrew can mean Job put himself above God, or simply that he claimed innocence before God.
b: Al tsaddeqo nafsho me'Elohim is literally "because he declared himself righteous from God." The preposition min can mean "rather than" or "more than" (KJV, most versions), so Job is charged with saving his own name at God's expense. It can also mean "before" or "in the face of" God, as in 4:17, which would only report Job's claim. The LORD himself later asks Job, "Would you declare me guilty so that you come out innocent?" (40:8), which suggests the stronger reading names a real danger.
orig: עַל־צַדְּקוֹ נַפְשׁוֹ מֵאֱלֹהִים (al tsaddeqo nafsho me'Elohim)

a: because the others were older than he was
p: In the ancient world the old spoke first. Elihu waited his turn and says so.
b: Wisdom in Israel and its neighbors belonged to the old: elders sat at the city gate and gave counsel (29:7–10). Eliphaz had leaned on this, telling Job that gray-haired men were on the friends' side (15:10), and Job himself had granted that wisdom goes with age (12:12). Elihu's opening speech (32:6–10) argues the opposite: wisdom is a gift of God's spirit, not of years. Proverbs makes the same point from both sides (Proverbs 16:31; 20:29).

a: to show you what I think
p: Elihu uses a word for "knowledge" that no one else in the Bible uses.
b: De'a, "knowledge, opinion," appears only in Elihu's speeches (32:6, 10, 17; 36:3), with the plural de'im in 37:16. He also likes the verb chawwah, "declare," which is common in Aramaic (32:6, 10, 17; 36:2). Scholars who think the Elihu speeches came from a different writer list words like these as evidence. Others answer that a poet can give a character his own way of talking, and that the whole of Job is full of rare words.

a: the spirit within a mortal
p: Either every human has God's breath, so even the young can be wise, or Elihu claims a prophet's inspiration.
b: Ruach means spirit, wind and breath; nishmat Shaddai, "the Almighty's breath," recalls God breathing life into the first human (Genesis 2:7; compare Job 27:3; Job 33:4). A general gift: Elihu says only that the spirit God gives every person, not age, is the source of understanding. A special gift: many Jewish and Christian readers hear a claim like the prophets', for whom the spirit came on chosen people (Numbers 11:25–29). The Talmud counts Elihu among seven prophets sent to the nations (Bava Batra 15b). An overclaim: readers who see him as pompous note that he calls this spirit a pressure in his belly (32:18).

a: Those with many years
p: Rabbim can mean the many, the great, or the old.
b: Rabbim usually means "many," so a literal rendering is "the many are not wise." In Aramaic and later Hebrew rab means a master or elder, and the parallel line has "the aged," so most versions take it as "the great" (KJV) or "the old in years." The Old Greek has "the long-lived." Either way Elihu's point is the same: years alone do not make a person wise.

a: God will rout him, not a human being
p: Elihu accuses the friends of giving up and saying only God can deal with Job. That is just what happens.
b: Yiddefennu comes from nadaf, "drive away," used of chaff and smoke blown off (Psalm 1:4; Psalm 68:2). Elihu imagines the friends excusing their silence: Job is beyond human answers, so God will have to rout him. Elihu means to do better. The irony is that the book ends exactly the way the friends supposedly said: God himself answers Job (38:1), and a human answer, Elihu's included, is passed over.

a: They are struck dumb; they answer no more
t: Who is Elihu talking to now?
p: Elihu stops saying "you" and starts saying "they." He seems to turn to an audience.
b: In 32:6–14 Elihu speaks to the three friends ("you" plural). In 32:15–16 he talks about them in the third person. Some readers think he turns to onlookers at the scene, perhaps the same "wise men" he addresses in 34:2. Others think he is talking to himself, or to the reader, an aside like one on a stage. In the Old Greek, 32:15–16 is missing and a new speech heading stands in place of 32:17 (see the note there), so the "they" of these lines does not exist in it. Scholars such as Carol Newsom note that Elihu acts like a listener who has heard the whole debate and now cannot stay in his seat.

a: the spirit in my belly squeezes me
p: Ruach is both spirit and wind. Readers have argued for centuries whether this line is inspired or funny.
b: A prophet's compulsion: Jeremiah felt God's word as a fire shut up in his bones that he could not hold in (Jeremiah 20:9), and Amos said no one can stop a prophet from speaking when God has spoken (Amos 3:8). On this view Elihu is a true messenger. A comic portrait: scholars such as William Whedbee and Norman Habel note that a belly full of wind recalls Eliphaz's taunt about a wise man who fills his insides with the east wind (15:2, where "insides" is the same Hebrew word, beten, "belly"), and Job's "Will words of wind ever stop?" (16:3). A young man so swollen with words that he will burst like a wineskin may be meant to make us smile.
orig: רוּחַ בִּטְנִי (ruach bitni), "spirit/wind of my belly"

a: it is about to burst like new wineskins
p: Fermenting wine gives off gas. A skin with no vent will split, even a new one.
b: Wine was stored in goatskins. While it ferments it gives off gas, so the skin needs a vent or room to stretch. Elihu says his belly is wine with no outlet, and even a new skin, which stretches best, would split. Jesus used the same everyday fact in a different way: new wine goes in new skins, because old ones would burst (Matthew 9:17; Mark 2:22; Luke 5:37–38). The Old Greek of Job has "like a skin of new wine boiling, bound up, or like a smith's bellows bursting."

a: Let me not play favorites with anyone
p: "Lifting the face" is courtroom language for partiality. Elihu also refuses to use flattering titles.
b: Nasa panim, "lift the face," means to show favor, a judge's sin (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17). Job had warned the friends not to show such favor even to God (13:8, 10). Kinnah in the next line means to give someone an honor-name (Isaiah 44:5; Isaiah 45:4). Elihu keeps his promise in a striking way: he is the only speaker who calls Job by his name (33:1, 31; 37:14).
orig: אַל־נָא אֶשָּׂא פְנֵי־אִישׁ ... לֹא אֲכַנֶּה (al-na essa fene-'ish ... lo akhanneh)

a: Now then, Job
p: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar never call Job by name. Elihu does it again and again.
b: In the long debate (chapters 4–27) the friends speak to Job but never use his name. Elihu addresses him as "Job" at 33:1, 33:31 and 37:14, and names him in the third person at 34:5, 34:7, 34:35–36 and 35:16. Some take this as frankness, keeping his promise not to flatter (32:21–22). Others hear a young man's lack of manners toward an elder. It also makes Elihu sound like a lawyer naming the other party.

a: God's spirit made me
p: Elihu echoes the creation of the first human and Job's own words about being made by God.
b: God formed the human from dust and breathed into him the breath of life (Genesis 2:7). Job had said the same of himself: God's hands shaped him (10:8–12), and God's breath was in his nostrils (27:3). Elihu uses this shared origin two ways: it is the source of his understanding (32:8), and it means he and Job are equals before God (33:6). Psalm 104:30 calls the spirit God's power to create and renew.

a: I am the same as you before God
t: "Like your mouth": an equal, or a spokesman?
p: Literally "I am like your mouth toward God." It may mean "just like you," or "the spokesman you asked for."
b: Hen ani khefikha la'El is literally "See, I am as your mouth to God." An equal: ke-fi often means "in proportion to, like," so most modern versions read "I am just like you before God," which the next line supports. A spokesman: the KJV reads "I am according to thy wish in God's stead," taking Elihu to offer himself as the go-between Job had begged for (9:33; 13:3, 20–22; 31:35). This second reading lies behind some Christian readings of Elihu as a forerunner of the mediator.

a: I too was nipped off from clay
p: The Hebrew verb is the same one Babylonian poems use for the gods pinching off clay to make humans.
b: Qorats means "nipped, pinched off." Its Akkadian cousin karatsu is the word used when the goddess Aruru "pinched off clay" to make the wild man Enkidu in the Epic of Gilgamesh, and when the birth goddess pinches off fourteen pieces of clay to make the first humans in Atrahasis. The Bible pictures God as a potter too (Genesis 2:7; Job 10:9; Isaiah 64:8). Verdict: a real shared image and a shared verb, not borrowing of a story. Elihu's point is humble: he is made of the same clay as Job.

a: my weight will not bear down on you
p: Job asked God to lift his hand and stop his terror. Elihu promises he brings neither.
b: Job had begged God, "Let him lift his rod off me, / and let his terror stop frightening me" (9:34; compare 13:21). Elihu takes up the same pair of ideas, dread and a heavy hand. Akhpi appears only here; it may mean "my pressure" or come from kaf, "palm, hand," which is how the Old Greek takes it ("my hand"). The message is: I am the hearing you asked for, without the terror.

a: I am pure and free of rebellion
p: Elihu quotes Job, but more sharply than Job spoke.
b: Job never said these exact words. He did insist he was blameless (9:21), not guilty (10:7), that his prayer was pure (16:17), and that he would hold to his integrity (27:5–6), and his oath (chapter 31) denies every kind of wrongdoing. But he also spoke of the sins of his youth (13:26) and asked, "Suppose I sinned: what do I do to you" (7:20). Zophar had summed up Job the same way (11:4). Fair readers note that Elihu, like the friends, turns a claim of innocence of any crime that deserved this into a claim of having no sin at all.

a: He clamps my feet in the stocks
p: Elihu quotes Job 13:27 almost exactly.
b: Job said to God, "You clamp my feet in the stocks; / you keep an eye on every path I take" (13:27). Elihu repeats it, changing only "you" to "he." "he treats me as an enemy of his" (33:10) likewise echoes 13:24 and 19:11. Elihu has listened closely. He quotes Job more often and more exactly than any other speaker, the way a lawyer reads from a transcript (compare Zophar in 11:4 and Eliphaz in 22:13–14).

a: because he does not reply to all of a person's words
p: The line can mean God does not answer people, or God does not explain himself.
b: Ki khol-devarav lo ya'aneh is "that all his words he does not answer." Reading 1: God does not answer any of a person's words, which is Job's complaint (19:7; 30:20). Reading 2: God does not give an account of any of his own doings (KJV "he giveth not account of any of his matters"). Either way, Elihu's reply is the same: God does speak, but people do not notice (33:14).
orig: כִּי כָּל־דְּבָרָיו לֹא־יַעֲנֶה (ki khol-devarav lo ya'aneh)

a: For God speaks one time
p: God is not silent. He speaks in dreams (33:15–18) and in sickness (33:19–30).
b: This is the heart of Elihu's first speech. Job has said God will not answer. The friends never directly took that on. Elihu does: God speaks twice over, first in warning dreams, then through pain that brings a person to the edge of death, and he sends a go-between to bring the person back. Many readers think this is Elihu's real advance on the friends. It treats suffering as a warning and a teaching, not only a penalty. The "one time ... a second time" pattern also appears in Psalm 62:11 and Job 40:5.

a: in a dream, a vision by night
p: Elihu borrows Eliphaz's words about a night vision, but draws a different lesson from them.
b: Eliphaz told of a voice that came "at the hour deep sleep falls on mortals" (4:13). Elihu repeats the Hebrew phrase exactly, and this site renders it the same way in both places. Tardemah, deep sleep, is also the sleep God sent on Adam (Genesis 2:21) and Abram (Genesis 15:12). Eliphaz's vision said that no mortal is righteous before God. Elihu's dream is a warning given so that a person can turn back in time, like Abimelech's dream (Genesis 20:3–7) or Pilate's wife's (Matthew 27:19).

a: his life from crossing the River
t: The sword, or the river of death?
p: Shelach can be a weapon or a channel. Many now hear a river of the underworld.
b: Me'avor ba-shelach is "from passing over by/into the shelach." A weapon: shelach means a javelin or missile (2 Chronicles 23:10; Joel 2:8), so the KJV has "from perishing by the sword." A channel: the same root gives the Shiloah channel and the Pool of Shelah (Isaiah 8:6; Nehemiah 3:15), and Mesopotamian poems speak of a river that the dead must cross. Pope and others read "from crossing the River," which fits "the Pit" in the parallel line. The same phrase returns in 36:12.

a: He holds his soul back from the Pit
p: Shachat, "the Pit," comes five times in this one speech.
b: Shachat is a pit or grave, another name for Sheol, the world of the dead (Psalm 16:10; Psalm 30:9). Elihu uses it at 33:18, 22, 24, 28 and 30: the whole passage is a rescue from the edge of the grave. Nefesh, here "soul," means the person's very life, not a soul apart from the body.

a: Or he is disciplined on his sickbed with pain
p: Elihu says sickness can be God speaking, to turn a person back before it is too late.
b: Hukhach, "he is corrected, rebuked," is a courtroom and classroom word. Eliphaz had already said that the one God corrects is fortunate (5:17), so the idea is not new. Elihu develops it: pain is a warning, it brings the sufferer to the edge of death, and God provides a way back. The strength of the view: it allows suffering to have a purpose without proving the sufferer wicked. The objection: the reader knows from chapters 1–2 that Job is not suffering for correction, and Elihu still assumes Job needs it. Proverbs 3:11–12 and Hebrews 12:5–11 take up the same theme.

a: the death-dealers
p: Memitim may be angels of death, or simply "the dead."
b: La-memitim is "to those who put to death." Many take them as angels who carry out death, like the destroyer at the Passover (Exodus 12:23) or the angel who struck Israel (2 Samuel 24:16). Others change one vowel to read le-metim, "to the dead." The Old Greek has "his life is in Hades." Either way, the next verse sets one good angel against them.

a: an angel standing by him
p: Mal'akh means "messenger." It can be a heavenly angel or a human sent by God.
b: Mal'akh is the ordinary word for a messenger, human (1:14) or heavenly (Genesis 19:1). Here it is a messenger "over" or "for" the dying man, who speaks up on his behalf. Most readers, ancient and modern, take it as an angel in God's court, the help Eliphaz had said Job could not find among "the holy ones" (5:1). Some think Elihu means a human messenger, perhaps himself.

a: a go-between
p: The same word names Joseph's interpreter, royal envoys, and the advocate Job hoped for.
b: Melits is a go-between: the interpreter between Joseph and his brothers (Genesis 42:23), envoys from Babylon (2 Chronicles 32:31), Israel's spokesmen before God (Isaiah 43:27). In 16:20 Job used the plural, melitsai, usually taken as "the ones who mock me" (as on this site), though some read "my go-betweens"; in the same breath he looked to a witness in heaven (16:19–21). He had also lamented that no umpire stood between him and God (9:33). Elihu answers that longing: there may be such a figure. The rabbinic Targum renders it "one advocate (peraqlit) among a thousand accusers."

a: one in a thousand
p: An angel advocate, a human teacher, or a figure of Christ. Each view has a long history.
b: An angel in the heavenly court. Most Jewish and modern readers. The Talmud builds on it: even if 999 angels argue against a person and one argues for him, he is saved (Shabbat 32a), and the Mishnah says each good deed gains a person an advocate (Avot 4:11). Maimonides called this angel Elihu's one new idea (Guide 3.23). A human messenger. A prophet or teacher who tells the sufferer the right way, perhaps Elihu. Christ. Many Christian readers see the one Mediator between God and humans (1 Timothy 2:5), who intercedes (Hebrews 7:25) and gives himself as a ransom (33:24; Mark 10:45). See the chapter page.

a: to tell a person where his uprightness lies
p: The go-between either teaches the sufferer what is right, or vouches for his uprightness to God.
b: Le-haggid le-adam yoshro is "to tell to a human his uprightness." Teaching: the messenger shows the person his duty, the way to be upright, so he can repent (KJV "to shew unto man his uprightness"). Vouching: the messenger testifies to God about the person's uprightness, like a defense witness. The Targum takes it as declaring the person's merit. The first reading fits Elihu's stress on warning and repentance; the second fits the courtroom picture.

a: I have come upon a ransom
p: Kofer is a price paid to spare a life. Elihu does not say what it is.
b: Kofer is the payment that ransoms a life otherwise forfeit (Exodus 21:30; Exodus 30:12). Psalm 49:7–8 says no one can pay God a ransom for another person's life. Elihu's speaker, the angel or God, says "I have found" one. Proposals: the person's suffering, his repentance, the angel's plea itself, or God's own mercy. Christian readers connect it with Jesus' words that he came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45; 1 Timothy 2:6). Elihu uses kofer again in 36:18. Pedahu, "spare him," is spelled oddly; it may be "redeem him" or "release him."

a: His flesh grows fresher than when he was a boy
p: Healing pictured as getting back a child's flesh.
b: Rutafash, "grows fresh," appears only here. The picture is like Naaman's healing, when his flesh came back like the flesh of a young boy (2 Kings 5:14). The rescue Elihu describes ends with full health, which is how Job's story will end too (42:10–17), though not by the path Elihu lays out.

a: he looks on God's face with shouts of joy
p: Healing leads to worship: the restored person comes before God with a festival shout.
b: Teru'ah is the shout of worship and festival (Psalm 27:6; Psalm 33:3). To "see God's face" means to come into his presence in worship (Psalm 11:7; Psalm 17:15). Job had longed to see God with his own eyes (19:26–27), and at the end he says he has (42:5). Elihu's picture ends where Job's story ends, but by a different road: repentance first, then the vision.

a: He sings out before others
p: Yashor may be "he sings" or "he looks." Either way, the healed person speaks in public.
b: Yashor 'al-anashim may come from shir, "sing" (most versions), or shur, "look on." The Old Greek has "he will blame himself." The picture matches the thanksgiving psalms, where a person who was rescued tells the assembly what God did and admits the sin that led to the trouble (Psalm 22:22–25; Psalm 32:3–5; Psalm 116:12–19). "I was not paid what I deserved" means God's mercy was greater than his punishment.

a: two times, three times over, with a person
t: Twice, three times, and no more?
p: The rabbis drew a rule of forgiveness from this line, and one medieval scholar found a hidden teaching in it.
b: The Talmud says that a person who commits the same sin is forgiven the first, second and third time, but not the fourth, reading this verse beside Amos's "for three sins, even four" (Yoma 86b; Amos 1:3). Nachmanides (Ramban) suggested that "to bring him back from the Pit" hints at a hidden teaching about the soul's return in a new life, an idea known in medieval Jewish mysticism. Most readers take the numbers simply: God gives more than one chance.

a: to light him up with the light of the living
p: Life before God is light; death is darkness.
b: Be'or ha-chayyim, "in the light of the living," appears also in Psalm 56:13, where the rescued person walks before God "in the light of the living." Job had described death as a land of gloom where even light is like darkness (10:21–22). Elihu's rescue ends in the opposite place.

a: I would like to clear your name
t: Does Elihu want Job to win?
p: Elihu says his goal is to show Job is righteous. Readers differ on whether to believe him.
b: Chafatsti tsaddeqekka is "I want to declare you righteous." Sincere: Elihu offers Job the chance to speak and hopes he can be shown right. His dream-and-sickness picture is a road back for Job. Hollow: he never actually pauses for Job, and by 34:36 he wishes Job "tested to the very end." Habel reads the line as part of a portrait of a young man who believes he is the arbiter Job called for. The line was not in the Old Greek (see 33:29).

a: You wise men
p: Elihu now speaks to a group. It may be the three friends, onlookers, or every reader.
b: The three friends: but Elihu has just said they failed (32:12), so the title would be ironic. Onlookers: elders and sages of the town, the kind of men who once listened to Job at the gate (29:7–10). Elihu calls them "you thoughtful men" (34:10) and expects "men of sense" to agree with him (34:34). The readers: the speech asks the audience to weigh Job's words and give a verdict. Elihu still speaks to Job directly at times (34:16, 33).

a: For the ear puts words to the test
p: Elihu quotes a saying Job used, and turns it against him.
b: Job had said, "The ear puts words to the test, does it not, / just as the mouth tastes food to eat?" (12:11). Elihu repeats it almost word for word. Job used it to say he could judge the friends' words for himself; Elihu uses it to invite his hearers to judge Job's.

a: I am righteous
p: Elihu strings together things Job really said.
b: Job did say "I know that I am the one who is right" (13:18), swore "By the life of God, who has stripped me of my right" (27:2), and vowed to hold on to his righteousness (27:6). "The arrow in me" recalls 6:4, where Job said the Almighty's arrows were in him. Elihu's quotations here are fairer than in 33:9.

a: Should I lie about my right?
t: A liar, or forced to lie?
p: Akhazzev can be "I am called a liar" or "Should I lie?"
b: Al-mishpati akhazzev can mean "in spite of my right I am counted a liar" or "Should I lie about my right?" The second fits Job's oath that he will not speak falsely by confessing what he did not do (27:4–6). The Old Greek has "he lied in my case," making God the liar. The verse shows why Job's words alarmed his hearers: he seems to say God has made him out a liar.

a: He gulps down mockery like water
p: Elihu borrows Eliphaz's picture of a man who drinks wrong like water.
b: Eliphaz had said a mortal is one who drinks injustice like water (15:16). Elihu applies the same picture to Job: he drinks in scorn, either scorning God or soaking up scorn from others. The next verse (34:8) goes further than anything Job did: it puts him in the company of evildoers, which Job had flatly denied (21:16; 31:5).

a: It gets a man nothing
p: Job never said this himself. He said the wicked say it.
b: The nearest Job came was to say that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike (9:22) and to quote the wicked, who ask what good it does to pray to the Almighty (21:15). Elihu takes Job's description of the wicked as Job's own creed. In fairness to Elihu, Job's argument does seem to lead there, and Elihu returns to it in 35:3. Malachi heard the same complaint in his day (Malachi 3:14).

a: God would never do wickedness
t: The Judge of all the earth
p: Elihu's whole second speech defends one claim: God cannot do wrong.
b: Chalilah, "far be it," is the same strong word Abraham used when he asked whether the Judge of all the earth would do what is unjust (Genesis 18:25). Moses' song says God's works are perfect and all his ways just (Deuteronomy 32:4). Elihu's argument is about God's nature: a God who did wrong would not be God, and the world would fall apart (34:13–15).

a: the Almighty does not twist what is right
p: Elihu repeats Bildad's question as an answer.
b: Bildad opened his first speech with "Does God twist justice? / Does the Almighty twist what is right?" (8:3). Elihu uses the same verb, 'awat, "bend, twist," with the same divine names, God and the Almighty (Shaddai). On this point the young man and the old friends agree. The LORD's question in 40:8 shows that the issue is real, though the LORD does not condemn Job the way they do.

a: draw his spirit and breath back into himself
p: Every breath depends on God. If he took his breath back, all flesh would die.
b: Psalm 104:29 says the same: when God takes away creatures' breath, they die and return to dust, and when he sends his spirit they are created. The line also looks back to the dust of Genesis 3:19 and ahead to Ecclesiastes 12:7. Elihu's argument: a God who keeps the whole world breathing has every reason to rule it well. Some read the first line "if he set his heart on him," meaning on a human being.

a: hold the reins
t: Can a hater of justice govern?
p: Chavash means to bind up, and so to rule.
b: Yachavosh comes from chavash, "bind, bandage, saddle." Here it means to govern, perhaps "to keep things bound together." Elihu's argument is that injustice and rule cannot go together; a world-ruler who hated justice would undo his own world. Job's reply would be that he sees exactly such a world (9:24; 24:1–12).

a: prefer the rich over the poor
p: God plays no favorites, a teaching that runs through the whole Bible.
b: Moses says God shows no partiality and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17). Proverbs says rich and poor meet together, and the LORD made them both (Proverbs 22:2). Peter learned that God shows no favoritism (Acts 10:34). Elihu uses shoa', "noble, rich," a rare word. The same letters appear in 36:19, where they may mean "your wealth" or, as this site takes them, "your cry for help."

a: though no hand touches them
p: The mighty fall without anyone lifting a finger.
b: "Not by a hand" is the same idea as the stone cut out "not by hands" that smashes the statue in Daniel 2:34, and the king who is broken "not by human hand" in Daniel 8:25. God's judgments do not need human agents. The night setting recalls the death of Egypt's firstborn at midnight (Exodus 12:29).

a: He does not set a man a further date
p: Job wanted a day in court with God. Elihu says God does not need one.
b: The Hebrew reads "he does not set upon a man further ('od)." Many scholars change one letter to read mo'ed, "a set time," which gives a clear sense: God does not schedule a hearing before he judges. Job had longed for such a hearing (9:32; 23:3–7) and asked why the Almighty does not set times (24:1). Elihu answers that God sees everything already (34:21–22), so no trial is needed.
orig: כִּי לֹא עַל־אִישׁ יָשִׂים עוֹד (ki lo 'al-ish yasim 'od)

a: So they made the poor cry out to him
p: God hears the oppressed. That is why he brings down their oppressors.
b: The law warns that if widows and orphans cry out to God, he will hear them (Exodus 22:22–23, 27), and God heard Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 3:7). James says the cries of cheated workers reach the Lord of Armies (James 5:4). Elihu agrees with Job that the poor cry out (24:12); he denies Job's charge that God takes no notice.

a: Suppose someone says to God
t: The hardest lines in the speech
p: Verses 29–33 are among the most uncertain in Job. Every translation guesses.
b: The Hebrew of 34:29–33 is short and its grammar unclear. Much of 34:25–33 was missing from the Old Greek and was filled in later from Theodotion, so the Greek gives little independent help. Our rendering takes 31–32 as an example of what a person might say in repentance, and 33 as Elihu's challenge: will God reward you on your own terms when you reject his? Other proposals: 30 may describe a godless ruler God sets over a sinful people; 31–32 may be a confession Elihu urges Job to make; 33 may mean "You must decide, not I." Clines lists more than a dozen ways to read these lines.

a: I wish Job were tested to the very end
p: The first word, avi, normally means "my father."
b: Avi yibbachen Iyyov begins with a word that usually means "my father." The Latin Vulgate reads it so: "My father, let Job be tried." Most interpreters take it as a word of wishing ("would that"), perhaps related to a similar word in 1 Samuel 24:11 or in other Semitic languages (KJV "My desire is that Job may be tried"). Either way, this is Elihu's harshest line: let Job be tested to the limit, because he talks like the wicked.

a: among us he claps in scorn
p: Clapping the hands was a gesture of contempt.
b: Yispoq is "he claps." In the Bible, clapping at someone is mockery (27:23; Lamentations 2:15). Elihu says Job's words amount to jeering at God in front of everyone. Some take the verb from an Aramaic root meaning "he doubles" his rebellion. Elihu's verdict on Job in this speech is the most severe he gives.

a: My rightness is greater than God's
p: Tsidqi me'El: "my righteousness is more than God's," or "I am right before God."
b: Like 32:2, the preposition min can mean "more than" or "before." Job never said he was more righteous than God, but he did say God was treating him unjustly (19:6–7; 27:2). Elihu reads that as the same thing. The LORD later asks something close: "Would you declare me guilty so that you come out innocent?" (40:8).

a: What do I gain more than if I had sinned?
p: Elihu returns to the charge of 34:9.
b: Job had asked why he should struggle in vain (9:29) and described the wicked who ask what profit there is in prayer (21:15). Elihu turns this into Job's own question: what is the use of being good? His answer (35:5–8) is that goodness does not change God, but it does matter to other people. The Old Greek lacked this verse: Jerome's Latin translation of the hexaplaric Greek marks it with Origen's asterisk, and Codex Vaticanus still lacks it. Other Greek manuscripts have it from Theodotion.

a: you and your friends along with you
p: The three, or everyone who thinks like Job.
b: "Your friends" (re'ekha) may be Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, which is odd, since they did not share Job's view. So many readers think Elihu means people of Job's opinion, or anyone who might agree with him, including the readers. The Greek of Codex Vaticanus, probably the Old Greek here, has "your three friends."

a: Look up at the sky and see
p: Elihu argues that God is too high to be helped or hurt by human sin or goodness.
b: Eliphaz had said much the same: can a man be of use to God, and does it give the Almighty pleasure if you are righteous? (22:2–3; compare 22:12). The strength of the view: God does not need anything from us, so his justice is not self-interested. The objection: it seems to make God distant, and Job's whole complaint was that God was too far away. Elihu's answer is that righteousness and wickedness do matter, to other humans (35:8).

a: who puts songs in the night
p: Zemirot can mean songs or protection.
b: Zemirot usually means songs (2 Samuel 23:1). A related word means strength or protection: Exodus 15:2 pairs "my strength" and zimrat, and Ugaritic dmr means "strength, protection." So the line may mean God gives songs in the dark times, or that he gives protection in the night. The Old Greek has neither: "who appoints night watches." The first reading inspired the picture of praise in suffering, like Paul and Silas singing in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25; compare Psalm 42:8; Psalm 77:6).

a: who gives us more teaching than the animals of the land
t: More than the animals, or by the animals?
p: The Hebrew can say God teaches us more than the animals, or teaches us through them.
b: Mallefenu mi-bahamot arets can mean "teaches us more than the beasts" (most versions) or "teaches us from the beasts." Job had told the friends to question the cattle and the birds and learn from them (12:7). If Elihu means "by the animals," he is turning Job's words around. The point either way: people who cry out only for relief, and not for God, act less wisely than they were made to.

a: God will not hear what is hollow
p: Elihu says God does not answer empty cries, cries for relief that never seek him.
b: Shaw' is emptiness, falsehood. Elihu's argument in 35:9–13 is that oppressed people cry out against their oppressors but never ask for God himself (35:10), so their cries are "hollow," and pride keeps them from being heard (35:12). Readers who defend Elihu find a real insight here about prayer. Readers who side with Job note that Job did seek God himself (23:3) and still was not answered, until chapter 38.

a: your lawsuit lies before him
p: Elihu uses the language of a trial: the case is filed, and Job must wait.
b: Din is a legal case. All through the book Job has spoken like a man bringing God to court: he has prepared his case (13:18), asked for a hearing (23:4), and signed his statement (31:35). Elihu tells him the case is already before God; he must wait. The Old Greek reads quite differently: "be judged before him, if you can praise him as he is."

a: folly
p: Pash appears only here. Its meaning is a guess.
b: Pash may mean folly, arrogance or excess, from Arabic and Aramaic cousins. Many scholars read pesha', "rebellion," with one letter added, as the Greek line, which Jerome's hexaplaric Latin marks with an asterisk as Theodotion's, seems to have (paraptoma, "transgression"). The Old Greek lacked 35:15–16. The KJV has "he knoweth it not in great extremity." The point is that God's patience is not ignorance.

a: without knowledge he piles up words
p: Elihu's verdict on Job is almost the first thing the LORD says in 38:2.
b: Elihu has said this twice (34:35; 35:16) and says it of the wicked in 36:12. When the LORD speaks, his first question is, "Who is this who blurs the plan / with words that have no knowledge in them?" (38:2). Most readers: God confirms Elihu's charge against Job, though not his whole argument, and God's verdict in 42:7 is more favorable to Job. A few readers: since Elihu has just finished speaking, the LORD's "who is this?" is aimed at Elihu. The Old Greek lacked 35:15–16, so this echo is missing there.

a: Wait for me a little
p: Katar, "wait," is Aramaic, one of several in Elihu's speeches.
b: Katar means "wait" in Aramaic, while in Hebrew the same root means "surround." Elihu's speeches have more words like this than the rest of Job: chawwah "declare" (32:6; 36:2), millin with an Aramaic plural (also elsewhere in Job), saggi' "great" (36:26). Scholars such as Driver and Gray counted them as signs of a different, later author. Gordis answered that Aramaic coloring suits a speaker from the land of Buz and the eastern setting of the whole book.

a: one whose knowledge is complete is here with you
p: Elihu says this about himself. In 37:16 he says the same thing about God.
b: Temim de'ot, "complete in knowledge," uses the same root as tam, the "wholehearted" Job of 1:1. In 37:16 the plural temim de'im describes God. Generous reading: Elihu means only that his knowledge is sound and sincere. Critical reading: he claims for himself what belongs to God, part of a portrait of a young man full of himself. Gregory the Great read Elihu as a picture of the proud within the church, who say true things in an arrogant way.

a: and rejects no one
p: The Hebrew seems to lack something. The Old Greek has God not rejecting "the innocent."
b: Literally: "See, God is mighty and does not reject; mighty in strength of heart." The object of "reject" is missing, and "mighty" is repeated. The Old Greek supplies "the innocent," and some scholars add "the pure in heart." The general sense is clear: God's power does not make him scornful. Job had said the opposite: God rejects the work of his hands (10:3).
orig: הֶן־אֵל כַּבִּיר וְלֹא יִמְאָס (hen-El kabbir welo yim'as)

a: he gives them seats on thrones beside kings
p: God raises the righteous, a theme from Hannah's song.
b: Hannah sang that God lifts the poor from the dust to seat them with princes (1 Samuel 2:8), and Psalm 113:7–8 repeats it. Eliphaz said God sets the lowly on high (5:11). Elihu's picture of the righteous enthroned is the life Job once had (29:25). At the end Job is restored, but not in the way Elihu expects.

a: held fast by the cords of misery
p: Chains as God's discipline, like King Manasseh's.
b: The picture of the proud put in fetters and set free when they listen fits the story of Manasseh, taken to Babylon in chains, who humbled himself and was restored (2 Chronicles 33:11–13). Psalm 107:10–16 tells of prisoners in iron who cried to the LORD and were freed. For Elihu, the chains are a classroom (36:9–10).

a: for discipline
p: Elihu's key word for suffering: training, correction, instruction.
b: Musar is the word Proverbs uses for a father's discipline and a teacher's instruction (Proverbs 1:2–3, 8; Proverbs 3:11). Elihu said God "puts his seal on their correction" (33:16), and now he "uncovers their ears" for it. To "uncover the ear" means to reveal something (1 Samuel 9:15; 1 Samuel 20:2). For Elihu, suffering is God whispering to a person who would not otherwise listen. The Old Greek lacked most of 36:5–11, so the earliest Greek readers did not have this teaching; Origen filled it in from Theodotion.

a: He frees the afflicted through their affliction
p: A wordplay: God rescues the 'ani by his 'oni.
b: Yechallets 'ani be'onyo plays on 'ani, "the afflicted," and 'oni, "affliction." The preposition be- can mean "in" or "by means of." Elihu means both: in their suffering God rescues them, and he uses the suffering to do it. This is the center of Elihu's teaching. Psalm 119:67 and 71 say it from the sufferer's side, and the New Testament takes up the theme (Romans 5:3–4; Hebrews 12:11; 2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

a: He was luring you, too,
p: Verses 16–20 are some of the hardest Hebrew in Job. Treat any translation as a guess.
b: Almost every word of 36:16–20 is uncertain. The verbs can be past ("he lured you"), future ("he will lure you"), or conditional. A "wide place" is freedom (Psalm 18:19; Psalm 31:8), and a full table is blessing (Psalm 23:5). Our reading: God was trying to draw Job out of trouble into blessing, but Job is preoccupied with the fate of the wicked (36:17). The Greek of 36:16, which Jerome's hexaplaric Latin marks as Theodotion's, is quite different: "an abyss, a downpour beneath it."

a: do not let a large ransom turn you aside
p: Kofer again: a price for a life, or a bribe.
b: Kofer is the "ransom" of 33:24, but it can also be a bribe (1 Samuel 12:3; Amos 5:12). Reading 1: do not let the high price of your suffering, the ransom that buys your rescue, drive you away. Reading 2: do not imagine that wealth or a bribe can buy your way out (this fits the "wealth" reading of 36:19; this site's plain text there follows "cry for help"). Chemah, "rage," may be Job's anger or God's.

a: Do not yearn for the night
p: Job's longing for death, or the night when God judges nations?
b: Death: Job wished the night of his conception had perished and longed for death (3:3–10; 7:4). Elihu may be warning him not to long for it. Judgment: in 34:20 and 34:25 the night is when God overthrows nations, so Elihu may be warning Job not to wish for God's judgment to fall. The second half of the verse is very obscure.

a: What teacher is like him?
p: Moreh, "teacher," comes from the same root as torah, "teaching."
b: Elihu has offered to teach Job (33:33). Now he points to the teacher no one can match. Isaiah promised Israel would see its Teacher (Isaiah 30:20), and the psalms ask God to teach his ways (Psalm 25:8–9; Psalm 94:10–12). The Old Greek reads "who is a ruler like him?", as if from a different word. This verse opens the hymn that leads into the storm (36:22–37:24).

a: Who has ever told him, 'You did wrong'?
p: God answers to no one. Isaiah and Paul say the same.
b: Job had said much the same in despair: "Who will ask him, 'What are you doing?'" (9:12). Elihu says it in praise. Isaiah asks who has directed the LORD's spirit or taught him (Isaiah 40:13–14), and Paul quotes that question (Romans 11:34). In 40:2 the LORD asks whether the faultfinder will contend with the Almighty.

a: they filter into rain from his mist
p: 'Ed, "mist," appears elsewhere only in Genesis 2:6.
b: 'Ed is the stream or mist that watered the ground before rain (Genesis 2:6). The verb zaqaq is used of refining or filtering. Elihu pictures God drawing up water and letting it fall as rain. Some modern readers find the water cycle here, as also in Ecclesiastes 1:7 and Amos 9:6. The text is poetry about God's care, built on close observation of the sky, not a theory of evaporation.

a: the thunder from his pavilion
p: The storm cloud as God's tent, from David's song.
b: Sukkah, "booth, pavilion," is God's covering of dark clouds in David's song: he made darkness his tent, thick clouds around him (2 Samuel 22:12; Psalm 18:11). Elihu's hymn now turns to the coming storm, and the LORD will speak out of a storm in 38:1. Many readers think Elihu is describing a real storm that is rolling in as he speaks.

a: This is how he rules over nations
p: Yadin means "judges"; a small change gives "feeds," to match the next line.
b: Yadin 'ammim is "he judges peoples." Some scholars read yazun, "he nourishes," which matches "hands out food in plenty." Without the change, the line says something Elihu repeats in 37:13: the same storm can bring judgment or harvest. Rain was life in a land that depended on it (Deuteronomy 11:13–17).

a: His roar gives notice of him
p: Translators disagree on almost every word of 36:33.
b: Literally: "Its noise declares about him; cattle also about what goes up." Our rendering takes it that the thunder announces God, and even the herds sense the storm rising. With other vowels the same letters can mean "stirring up anger against wrongdoing." The Greek, which is Theodotion's (the Old Greek lacked 36:29–37:5), read re'o as "his friend" and miqneh as "possession": "He will declare about it to his friend; the Lord is a possession, also concerning injustice." Every version here is a best guess.
orig: יַגִּיד עָלָיו רֵעוֹ מִקְנֶה אַף עַל־עוֹלֶה (yaggid 'alav re'o miqneh af 'al-oleh)

a: At this my heart pounds too
p: Elihu's heart pounds at the thunder. Many readers think the storm of 38:1 is arriving.
b: A real storm: Elihu's hymn moves from rain (36:27) to thunder and lightning (36:29–37:5), and here he reacts as if he hears it. Out of this storm the LORD speaks (38:1). On this reading Elihu is a herald, like a forerunner announcing the king. Poetic description: others think Elihu is only describing a typical storm, and the link to 38:1 is the poet's, not the scene's. Either way, the book places Elihu's last words right before the voice from the storm. In the Old Greek most of 36:29–37:5, the thunder passage, was missing; it came into Greek manuscripts from Theodotion.

a: Hear it, all of you
p: Elihu now speaks to all who are listening, not just to Job.
b: Shim'u shamoa', "listen, listen," is plural. Elihu has turned from Job (36:16–21, singular) to everyone present, as in 34:2. In 37:14 he will speak to Job alone again. Qol, "voice," is also the Hebrew word for thunder, so "his voice" here is the thunder.

a: he thunders with his voice of majesty
p: Canaanite poems praise Baal's thunder. Israel's poets gave that voice to the LORD alone.
b: In the Ugaritic Baal Cycle (about 1300 BC), the storm god Baal "gives his voice" from the clouds, and the earth shakes. Psalm 29 uses the same imagery of the LORD's voice over the waters, breaking cedars and shaking the wilderness. Verdict: a real shared image. Israel's poets used the language of the storm god to say that it is the LORD, not Baal, who rules the storm. Elihu's hymn stands in that tradition, and the LORD's speeches will claim the weather as his own (38:22–38).

a: To the snow he says, 'Fall to the ground,'
p: Hewe' is a rare, Aramaic-looking word, perhaps "fall."
b: Hewe' arets may be "be on the earth" (Aramaic hwh, "be") or "fall to earth" (Arabic hawa, "fall"). Snow was rare and striking in Israel's hill country (2 Samuel 23:20; Psalm 147:16). The LORD will soon ask Job whether he has seen where snow is stored (38:22).

a: He stamps a seal on every human hand
p: Most take it as winter stopping work. The Talmud read it as a person signing for his deeds at death.
b: Winter: snow and rain shut down outdoor work, so people stay inside and see God's work instead of their own (compare the animals in 37:8). A signature: the Talmud says that when a person dies, all his deeds are read out before him and he signs the record, citing this verse: God seals the hand of every person (Ta'anit 11a). The Greek, which Jerome's hexaplaric Latin marks with an asterisk and so is probably Theodotion's, has "so that every person may know his own weakness."

a: cold from the winds that scatter
p: Mezarim may be north winds that scatter clouds, or a name for stars.
b: Mezarim looks like "scatterers," perhaps the north winds that clear the sky and bring cold. It may be connected with mazzarot (38:32), a star group, and the "chamber" with "the hidden rooms of the south" (9:9). The Vulgate has "from Arcturus cold," and the KJV "out of the north."

a: or for loyal love
p: The same storm can be God's rod of discipline or a gift of hesed.
b: Shevet is a rod, the rod of discipline, and hesed is "loyal love," God's covenant faithfulness. The two appear together in God's promise to David: he will punish with a rod, but his loyal love will not leave (2 Samuel 7:14–15; Psalm 89:32–33). Elihu's point is the heart of his teaching: the same storm, like the same suffering, can be punishment or love, and God decides which.

a: Stand still and take a hard look at the wonders of God
p: Elihu's "Do you know...?" questions (37:15–18) sound like the LORD's in chapters 38–39.
b: "Stand still and see" is what Moses said at the sea (Exodus 14:13) and Samuel said before a storm (1 Samuel 12:16–18). Elihu's next questions, "Do you know?" and "Can you?", sound like a preview of the LORD's: "Do you know the season when the ibex of the crags give birth?" (39:1). Readers who see Elihu as a forerunner point to this. Readers who think he was added later suggest he was written to prepare for the divine speeches.

a: hammering out the skies
t: A sky like a metal mirror
p: The verb is the root of raqia, the "dome" of Genesis 1.
b: Tarqia' means to beat out metal into a sheet (Exodus 39:3; Isaiah 40:19). From the same root comes raqia', the "dome" or "firmament" of Genesis 1:6–8. Ancient mirrors were polished bronze (Exodus 38:8). Elihu pictures the hot summer sky as a hard, shining sheet. Readers differ on whether this is poetic picture or reflects an ancient belief in a solid sky.

a: Would anyone ask to be swallowed whole?
p: Elihu says a person who asked for a hearing with God would be destroyed. Then God speaks.
b: Elihu's point: Job has demanded a hearing (31:35), but who would ask to talk to God, knowing it would swallow him up? The irony is sharp. In the next chapter God speaks to Job, and Job is not destroyed. Instead, Job says that now his eye has seen God (42:5). Yevulla' can also mean "be confused," which some prefer here.

a: From the north comes gold
p: The north was the home of the gods in Canaanite poems, and of storms in Israel.
b: Tsafon, "north," was also the name of Mount Zaphon, the home of Baal in Ugaritic poems. The Bible borrows the name for God's holy mountain (Psalm 48:2; Isaiah 14:13). Ezekiel's vision of God came in a storm from the north, with a gleam like metal (Ezekiel 1:4). "Gold" may be the golden light after a storm, or golden splendor around God. The Old Greek has "clouds shining like gold." Verdict: the poem uses old imagery for the place of divine glory, without adopting the myth.

a: The Almighty we cannot reach
p: Elihu's closing words echo Job's search for God.
b: Job had cried, "Would that someone could tell me how to find him" (23:3) and said he could not find God in any direction (23:8–9). Zophar had asked whether Job could find out the limits of the Almighty (11:7). Elihu ends on the same note: lo metsa'nuhu, "we have not found him." A moment later the LORD finds Job (38:1).

a: he crushes no one
t: He does not oppress, or does not answer?
p: The same consonants can mean "he does not afflict" or "he does not answer."
b: The Masoretic vowels read lo ye'anneh, "he does not afflict, oppress": God's justice does not crush. With other vowels the word is ya'aneh, "he does not answer," which would sum up Job's complaint and set up the surprise of 38:1, where the LORD "answered Job." The Old Greek supports the second sense: "You who judge rightly, do you not think he listens?" Most versions still follow the Masoretic reading.

a: he has no regard for any of the wise of heart
p: Elihu's last line can praise or warn. It may even cut against Elihu.
b: "Wise of heart" is usually praise (Exodus 31:6; Proverbs 16:21). Here God "does not see" them, so most take it as "those wise in their own eyes" (KJV "wise of heart"; compare Proverbs 3:7; Isaiah 5:21). Some read "all the wise of heart cannot see him." Readers who see Elihu as pompous note that his last words condemn self-made wisdom, just before God speaks to the man Elihu was sure he could teach.

a: I will give my share of the answer, I too
t: The Old Greek starts a second speech here
p: The Old Greek has no 32:15–16. In place of 32:17 it reads "And Elihu went on and said."
b: Origen marked 32:15–16 and most of 32:11–12 with asterisks: the Old Greek translator, working in the 100s BC, left them out, and Origen added them from Theodotion. Where the Hebrew has 32:17, the Old Greek has a speech heading, Hypolabon de Elious legei, "And Elihu went on and said," followed by "I will speak again." So in the earliest Greek, Elihu's opening is two speeches, the first to the friends and the second beginning at 32:18, where Elihu says he is full of words. Codex Vaticanus still prints the heading, "And Elihu went on and said," right after the added lines.

a: See, all this is God's doing
t: Where the Old Greek's first speech ends
p: The Old Greek lacked much or all of 33:28–33. Its first Elihu speech ends with the sick man's confession.
b: Origen's asterisks, as Jerome's Latin translation of the hexaplaric Greek keeps them, mark 33:28–29 and 33:32–33 as lines the Old Greek did not have. Jerome leaves 33:30–31 unmarked, in a shorter form; other hexaplaric witnesses may mark these too, which this site has not been able to check. Either way the earliest Greek readers had no closing appeal to Job ("I would like to clear your name," 33:32). The Greek of 33:28, about a soul saved and a life that sees light, is Theodotion's, not the Old Greek's.

a: and to shield a man from pride
p: Yekhasseh means "he covers." Many scholars change one letter to read "he cuts off" pride.
b: The Hebrew is literally "and pride from a man he covers," which may mean God hides pride away from him, keeps it out of his reach. Many scholars read yekhalleh, "he puts an end to," or a similar verb, giving "to cut off pride from a man." The Old Greek has a different line: "and he rescued his body from falling."

a: Can your cry for help
p: Shu'akha can mean "your cry for help" or "your wealth." The whole verse is uncertain.
b: Haya'arokh shu'akha lo vetsar is literally "Will your shu'a set in order, not in distress?" Shua' means "a cry for help" in 30:24, while the similar shoa' means "rich, noble" in 34:19. So the line may ask whether Job's cry for help (this site's reading) or his wealth (KJV "Will he esteem thy riches?") can keep him out of trouble. The Old Greek has a quite different line: "Let not your mind willingly turn you away from the prayer of the helpless in distress."
orig: הֲיַעֲרֹךְ שׁוּעֲךָ לֹא בְצָר (haya'arokh shu'akha lo vetsar)
